core_content.body_markdown:
## Considerations when establishing resource needs

- Life cycle approach (linear, iterative or hybrid).
- Activities and tasks to be completed.
- Resource types required.
- Skill sets and capabilities.
- Critical tasks.
- Timeframe resources are needed.
- Project vs BAU needs.
- External resource requirements.

## Resources as constraints

Resources drive pace as well as cost. They can constrain what can be done and when, and constrain logistics through the space needed to operate and store items.

## Working with resource managers

Project managers secure resources through resource managers (often line managers in BAU). External resources come via supplier resource managers. Negotiation and a clear RACI keep this working.

## From OBS to RACI

The OBS lists the project organisation. Combined with the WBS (which lists the tasks), the PM produces a RACI matrix to allocate responsibility for each task.

| Letter | Meaning | Practical test |
|---|---|---|
| R - Responsible | Does the work, owns the problem | The 'doer' |
| A - Accountable | Approves the work, held to account | The 'sign-off' |
| C - Consulted | Provides input; two-way dialogue | The 'expert' |
| I - Informed | Kept up to date; one-way communication | The 'audience' |

## Best practice

One person Responsible and one person Accountable per task. More than one Accountable creates conflict; more than one Responsible diffuses ownership. Consulted and Informed can be plural.

## What the RACI does for the project

- Clarifies roles and responsibilities.
- Streamlines resource allocation.
- Supports task delegation.
- Acts as a reference for team and resource managers.

## Four resource categories

| Category | Examples |
|---|---|
| Human | People and their skills |
| Materials | Consumable inputs (concrete, steel, raw materials) |
| Plant or equipment | Machinery, tools |
| Facilities | Sites, offices, warehouses |

## When allocating, consider

- Resource type.
- Quantity per type.
- Availability against the schedule.
- Cost.

## Linear vs iterative allocation

| Aspect | Linear | Iterative |
|---|---|---|
| Planning assumption | All resources available when scheduled | Pre-allocated resource pool within each timebox |
| If resources don't fit | Apply smoothing or levelling | Vary scope or quality within the iteration |
| Risk | Schedule slip if resources unavailable | Under- or over-utilisation if work doesn't fit |

In linear, the schedule drives resourcing. In iterative, the resource pool drives what can be delivered each iteration.
core_content.outcome_title: Categorising and allocating resources by life cycle

core_content.body_markdown:
## The named distinction

| Technique | End date | Used when | How |
|---|---|---|---|
| Smoothing | Protected (does not change) | Time is more important than cost | Add more resources to reduce task durations; avoid peaks and troughs; parallelise non-dependent activities |
| Levelling | May change (end date can slip) | Resource is fixed and time can flex | Redefine scope, increase task durations, shift non-critical activities, bring earlier resources forward |

## The two questions to remember

- Smoothing answers: 'What resources do I need to deliver the work within the fixed timescale?'
- Levelling answers: 'With the resources available, when will the work be finished?'

## When neither is enough

If resources are genuinely finite, the project end date must extend. No smoothing technique can manufacture capacity that does not exist.

core_content.body_markdown:
## From estimate to budget

Estimates feed the budget. They support three jobs at once: setting the budget, judging value for money on the chosen solution, and feeding the resource schedule that produces the cost view of the project.

When creating a budget, consider:

- **Cost types and timing** so you know when funding drawdowns are needed to cover payment milestones.
- **External information** like supplier quotes and how they align to the plan.
- **Underlying assumptions** so they can be tested and rebudgeted if wrong.

## The Cost Breakdown Structure (CBS)

The CBS is built directly from the WBS. Take each work package, identify all activity with a cost, and attach the cost.

Costs attach to People, Equipment, Materials, and Other resources. The CBS uses the organisation's financial coding for booking and reporting.

## The four cost pairs to know cold

| Pair | Difference | Worked example |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed vs Variable | Fixed does not change with usage; variable does | Supplier flat retainer (fixed) vs concrete per cubic metre (variable) |
| Direct vs Indirect | Direct ties to project outputs; indirect is overhead | Site labour (direct) vs head-office rent share (indirect) |
| Recurring vs Non-recurring | Recurring hits periodically; non-recurring hits once | Monthly software licence (recurring) vs server purchase (non-recurring) |
| Capital vs Operational | Capital is asset spend; operational is running cost | New machinery (capex) vs maintenance contract (opex) |

## Why life cycle shapes the budget

- **Linear life cycle**: funds release at decision gates once spend to date and forecasts are approved. Larger, less frequent drawdowns.
- **Iterative life cycle**: shorter cycles, more frequent funding releases as work is completed in increments.
core_content.outcome_title: Creating a budget and the Cost Breakdown Structure

core_content.body_markdown:
## What cost control is for

Cost control identifies variances between forecast and actual so the project can act on them. Specifically, it:

- Minimises costs where possible.
- Identifies overspend areas.
- Corrects unacceptable overspend.
- Feeds lessons learned to future projects.

When the baseline changes (approved change request), update the cost information so forecasts stay credible.

## Earned Value Management in plain English

EVM answers three questions at once: How much did we plan to have done by now? How much have we actually done? How much did it cost?

- **Planned Value (PV)**: what you said the work scheduled by today should cost.
- **Earned Value (EV)**: what the work you have actually completed was budgeted to cost.
- **Actual Cost (AC)**: what you have actually spent.

From these three, two ratios:

- **CPI = EV / AC**: efficiency of spend. Above 1 is good (under budget for the work done).
- **SPI = EV / PV**: productivity vs schedule. Above 1 is good (ahead of plan).

## When EVM works and when it does not

EVM needs measurable progress and a stable baseline. It is excellent for construction, manufacturing and other projects where progress can be objectively quantified. It is not very useful in social impact projects where outcomes are qualitative, baselines are fuzzy and progress is hard to measure in money terms. Examiners specifically test this distinction.

## The Earned Value graph

If EV is below PV at today's date, you are behind schedule. If AC is above EV, you are over budget for the work done.
core_content.outcome_title: Cost control and Earned Value Management

core_content.body_markdown:
## What good monitoring looks like

The project manager and sponsor agree the monitoring approach early. Monitoring compares actual performance against the baseline; reports drive decisions.

Typical financial reports include:

| Report | Tells you |
|---|---|
| Actual vs forecast cost | Whether spend is tracking the plan |
| Actual vs forecast spend curve | Cumulative pattern over time |
| EVM report (EV, AC, PV, CPI, SPI) | Efficiency of spend and schedule productivity |
| Forecast cost overrun at completion | Where the project will land vs budget |
| Cashflow and drawdown report | When money is needed |
| Resource cost report | Where labour and equipment spend is going |
| Change request cost report | Cost impact of approved changes |
| Contingency drawdown report | Use of risk budget |
| Benefits realisation report | Whether the spend is producing value |

Monthly reporting with a traffic-light (RAG) format flags areas in or outside agreed tolerance.

## Reporting at governance reviews

Financial performance is also monitored through governance touchpoints: decision gates, benefit reviews, stage reviews, audits, post-implementation reviews. Any of these are valid answers to 'name a review point where you would report on financial performance'.

## Why closure deserves its own attention

Unclosed contracts and unclosed cost codes leak money. Closure is not paperwork; it is the difference between returning unused budget to the business and quietly continuing to spend it.

## The closure checklist

1. **Check no outstanding contract commitments** including overheads or standing costs, so the project is not over-charged.
2. **Reassign resources** back into the business, to the supplier, or out of the organisation.
3. **Formally close contracts** with the supply chain. Confirm all deliverables received and obligations met. Agree final accounts.
4. **Update accounting and management systems**. Close the project on the books, remove delegated authorities, close cost codes so no further money can be charged.
5. **Return surplus funding** to the business for use elsewhere.
6. **Submit the project closure report** to the final decision gate for endorsement.

Plan closure activities early in the life cycle so you do not incur uncosted closedown effort.

## Why this is the sponsor's moment

Closure activities are owned by the project sponsor with the project manager executing. The sponsor signs off the final accounts and endorses the closure report.

core_content.body_markdown:
## Benefits of risk management

- More realistic plans, schedules and budgets.
- Higher likelihood of schedules and budgets being kept.
- More accurate contingency allocation.
- Continuous learning and improvement.
- Greater stakeholder confidence.
- Threats minimised, opportunities maximised.

## Benefits of issue management

- Structure and escalation routes for timely resolution.
- Senior visibility for issues needing organisational resource.
- Consistent documentation for assessment.
- Re-prioritisation and decision-making support.
- Continuous learning and improvement.

## Contingency vs management reserve

| | Contingency | Management reserve |
|---|---|---|
| For | Identified (known) risks | Unidentified or very-low-probability high-impact risks (unknown unknowns) |
| Owner | Project manager (with sponsor approval to draw down) | Sponsor or governance board |
| Typically expressed in | Time and budget | Time, budget, sometimes scope/quality in iterative |

Contingency is not hidden padding. It is openly identified to cover the gap between the plan and known risks.
core_content.outcome_title: Benefits of risk/issue management and contingency planning

core_content.body_markdown:
## Risk management process

Initiation (set up the risk management plan), then:

1. **Identification**: surface risks using SWOT, brainstorming, checklists, prompt lists, assumption/constraint analysis. Log with owner.
2. **Analysis**: qualitative (probability/impact grid) and/or quantitative (Monte Carlo, decision trees, sensitivity analysis) to assess impact on objectives.
3. **Monitoring and escalation**: track triggers and thresholds; escalate when tolerance is breached.
4. **Response**: select proactive or reactive response; consider secondary and residual risk.
5. **Closure**: close in register when no longer a risk; capture lessons learned; communicate remaining risks at handover.

## Issue management process

1. **Log and analyse**: record in issue register, prioritise against success criteria, scope, time, cost, benefits.
2. **Escalate**: to sponsor and, if needed, governance board.
3. **Assign actions**: to the person or group best placed to resolve.
4. **Apply change control**: if the issue changes scope or baseline, route via change control to update plans.

## How life cycles differ

- **Linear**: risks and issues drive change control; updates the baselined plan.
- **Iterative**: risk-based mindset shapes design of each iteration; risks reviewed per iteration; scope or quality may flex inside the timebox.
core_content.outcome_title: The risk and issue processes (and how life cycle changes them)

core_content.body_markdown:
## Seven named responses

| Type | Threats | Opportunities |
|---|---|---|
| Proactive | Avoid (change cause), Reduce (lower probability/impact), Transfer (pass to another party) | Exploit (make it happen), Enhance (raise probability/impact), Share (collaborate) |
| Reactive | Accept (live with it; contingency if it lands) | Reject (decline the opportunity) |

## What each does

- **Avoid**: change objectives or practices so the cause no longer exists.
- **Reduce / Mitigate**: lower probability or impact.
- **Transfer**: assign responsibility to another party (insurance, contract clause).
- **Accept**: no viable proactive response; manage residual via contingency.
- **Exploit**: change practices to make the opportunity certain.
- **Enhance**: increase the likelihood or impact of the opportunity.
- **Share**: collaborate with another party to capture the opportunity.
- **Reject**: decline because value is low or effort too high.

## Two things to watch when responding

- **Secondary risks**: a new risk introduced by the response.
- **Residual risk**: what remains after the response. Must still be managed.
core_content.outcome_title: Risk responses: threats and opportunities, proactive and reactive

core_content.body_markdown:
## What governance brings

- Clear roles, responsibilities and delegated authority.
- Defined risk thresholds aligned to organisational appetite and tolerance.
- Escalation routes when thresholds are breached.
- Assurance targeted where the greatest risks lie.
- Consistent treatment across the portfolio for meaningful reporting and lessons.
- Stakeholder confidence in the project's ability to manage risk.

## What governance does NOT do

- It does not prevent risks from occurring (early detection helps; it doesn't eliminate).
- It does not stop the PM from making timely decisions; it sets the boundary within which they decide.

The relationship between governance, risk and assurance is reciprocal: governance sets the rules, risk analysis tells assurance where to look, assurance evidence improves risk assessment and decisions at gates.
core_content.outcome_title: Why governance matters in risk and issue management

worked_example.scenario: You are PM on a new luxury housing development. During analysis, the team identifies that the site is regularly hit by poor winter weather, which could delay the project and increase costs. You log the risk in the register. Justification: the risk is high-probability over the build duration, and the financial impact (delayed sales, holding costs) is significant. Transfer matches the risk profile and aligns to the sponsor's risk appetite. (b) Avoid was considered (relocate the project) but rejected because it changes the project's core proposition and the strategic intent is to develop on this site; the cost of avoidance exceeds the value. (c) Governance matters because it sets the risk thresholds the project operates within (aligned to organisational risk appetite), defines escalation routes when weather variance exceeds tolerance, ensures the risk is reported consistently for portfolio learning, and gives assurance the right place to look for the project's biggest exposures.

quick_recap: Change control protects the baseline. Unmanaged change is the biggest single cause of project failure.
Five stages: Request, Initial evaluation, Detailed evaluation, Recommendation, Update and implement.
Linear vs iterative: linear runs change as an exception; iterative embeds it in iteration planning.
A good CR captures source, reason, impact areas, owner, status, decision and justification.
After approval, update baselines, business case, risk register, configuration records and communicate.

core_content.body_markdown:
## The five stages

| Stage | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Request | CR is logged on the change register with a unique ID, owner, source and reason |
| Initial evaluation | Quick filter: is this worth detailed assessment? Considers necessity, feasibility, high-level impact |
| Detailed evaluation | Full impact on baseline success criteria, business case, completed work, other projects and BAU |
| Recommendation | Sponsor or governance board decides: Approve, Reject or Defer |
| Update plans and implement | Update baselines, business case, risk register, configuration records; communicate; implement and monitor |

## What approve / reject / defer mean

- **Approve**: the value of the change exceeds the cost of implementing it.
- **Reject**: cost or risk exceeds value, or the change goes beyond agreed thresholds.
- **Defer**: further clarification or information needed before a decision can be made.

## Linear vs iterative life cycles

| Aspect | Linear | Iterative |
|---|---|---|
| Scope/quality | Fixed | Flexible |
| Time/cost | Flexible | Fixed |
| Change handling | Formal CR process; controlled and exception-based | Embedded in iteration planning meetings; expected and routine |
| Decision route | Sponsor / governance board via formal recommendation | Product owner with team at iteration start |
| Documentation | Heavier; configuration baseline maintained | Lighter; backlog reprioritised |

Use the APM terms 'linear' and 'iterative'. Do not write 'waterfall' or 'agile' in the exam.

## Why structure matters

Unmanaged change is the single biggest cause of project failure. A retrospective process (after-the-fact CR) can be used if change was implemented without formal agreement, but this is a fallback, not the goal. A change freeze can protect delivery near critical milestones.

core_content.body_markdown:
## The change request form

A good CR captures enough for an informed decision and leaves a clean audit trail.

| Field | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Project overview | Context for evaluators not embedded in the team |
| Description of the change | What is being proposed |
| Reason for the change | Why now: regulation, risk, customer demand, financial driver |
| Areas impacted | First-pass scope of the change |
| Source of change | Who raised it; internal or external |
| Change request owner | Who is accountable for progressing the CR |
| Date raised and unique identifier | Audit trail |
| Status | Where the CR is in the process |
| Decision, date and justification | Outcome and reasoning |

Optional but useful: priority, approval level, proposed solution, follow-up actions, initial and detailed evaluation summaries.
core_content.outcome_title: What goes in a change request

core_content.body_markdown:
## What a change can affect

- Benefits
- Scope
- Schedule
- Costs
- Quality
- Resources
- Risks
- Stakeholders

Evaluation needs to test the proposal against the project's success criteria from the business case. It also asks: do we have the skills and resources to deliver this? Is the assessment effort itself proportionate to the change?

## Source matters

Understanding why the CR has been raised shapes how it is assessed. Is it mandatory (regulation), risk-driven, customer-driven, or financial? A mandatory regulatory change has different decision dynamics from a customer wishlist.

## Questions to answer when justifying a recommendation

1. Which areas of the project will be affected and how?
2. Do we have the skills and resources to handle it, or do we need external support?
3. Is there enough contingency budget to drawdown, or do we need to request more funding?
4. Does it affect the end date? If yes, are the outcomes still useful to the business?
5. Are the business case benefits materially impacted? How and why does that matter?

A strong recommendation links each of these to evidence and a clear conclusion.

## Why updating the plan matters

If the plan is not updated after an approved change, the team works from outdated information. Time and money are wasted. Conflict and disengagement follow. The delivered outputs may end up redundant. Stakeholders lose confidence. Other projects or BAU are affected.

Ultimately, the business case benefits may not be realised.

## What gets updated

- Baselined scope, schedule, cost and quality plans.
- Business case (if benefits or affordability shift).
- Risk register (new risks raised by the change).
- Configuration records (latest document versions).
- Roles and responsibilities.
- Communications plan.

## Communicating the change

The sponsor is accountable for ensuring the decision is communicated. The PM ensures all affected stakeholders receive the updated information, and that the team and supply chain understand the revised expectations.

Approve / Reject / Defer are the three recommendations. Defer = need more information. State this explicitly.
When asked about impacts of unmanaged change, name 'the benefits in the business case may not be realised'. This is the examiner's preferred closing phrase.

worked_example.scenario: You are project manager on a £2.5m office fit-out. The agreed plan included a conference room for 18 people plus three one-to-one video pods. The HR Manager has raised a CR to install video conferencing in the conference room itself because the Customer Services team now operates hybrid. Initial evaluation suggests the change is feasible. The Finance Manager has pushed back, arguing one team's needs should not change a major design decision. You are nine weeks from handover.

Matters because nine weeks out, contingency is thin. (2) Impact on schedule: AV install may push the AV contractor onto the critical path. Matters because handover slippage triggers penalty clauses. (b) Two justification questions: (1) Are there alternative options (use the pods for hybrid attendance) that avoid changing the design? (2) Is the change supported by a business need broad enough to justify the cost, or does it serve a single team? (c) Plans to update: revised cost plan and contingency drawdown report; revised schedule with the AV install activity; updated configuration record for the conference room design; updated risk register if the change adds critical-path risk.

diagrams.heading: Three life cycles to know

core_content.body_markdown:
## Three life cycles to know

| Life cycle | Features | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| Linear | Sequential with clearly defined outputs at each phase | Stable, low-risk projects where scope is well understood upfront |
| Iterative | Repeats one or more phases | Evolving scope or solutions; agile-style development |
| Hybrid | Iteration inside a linear backbone | Mixed projects where parts are stable and parts are evolving |

## Why linear life cycles use phases

- Clearer identification of priorities and focus on current work.
- Early definition of requirements (time spent on planning).
- Better stakeholder communication via regular project reviews.
- Maximum transparency through assessment against requirements at predefined milestones.
- Maximum control and governance.

Projects structured as phases also pass information forward cleanly at each milestone, reducing handover errors.
core_content.outcome_title: Linear, iterative and hybrid life cycles

core_content.body_markdown:
## What each contains

| Project life cycle | Extended life cycle |
|---|---|
| Concept -> Definition -> Deployment -> Transition and close | Same plus Adoption and Benefits Realisation |
| Accountability handed over at closure | Project team supports embedding; accountability stays with the project until change is embedded |
| Suits supplier-to-customer arrangements (contract ends at handover) | Suits internally-funded business change (benefits matter) |

## Why pick extended

Extended life cycles are right when the project is making a change to the business and benefits realisation matters. Adoption and benefits realisation are the two phases added on top of the standard project life cycle.

## When organisations favour linear

- Highly structured, predictable, stable process needed.
- Reasonably complete knowledge available upfront.
- Resistance to change; low tolerance for rework.
- Teams divided into distinct phases with handover boundaries.
- Lower appetite for risk.

## When organisations favour iterative

- Agile development projects.
- Departments that are flexible, adaptable, open to change.
- Concurrency / simultaneous engineering possible.
- Uncertainty about scope; objectives evolve with learning.
- Prototypes, timeboxes or parallel activities needed to acquire insights.

When choosing, also consider the deployment approach, desired benefits and outcomes, and the organisation's appetite for change. Predictive life cycles assume strong upfront knowledge; iterative life cycles facilitate knowledge creation as work progresses.
core_content.outcome_title: Context, culture and influence on choice

core_content.body_markdown:
## Quick-reference grid

| Life cycle | Strengths | Limitations |
|---|---|---|
| Linear | Suitable for low-risk projects; clear framework; maximum control and governance | Needs early clarity on scope; longer to first benefit; less flexible to change |
| Iterative | Suits vague scope; allows iterative feedback; integrates change more easily | Duration and cost less certain upfront; resource management more complex; business case harder to justify if scope vague |
| Hybrid | Mix of approaches tailored to the work; flexibility plus control | Requires skill and clarity using multiple systems of working in parallel |

## How to answer 'which life cycle' questions

1. Name the life cycle (1 mark).
2. Give three reasons it fits the context (3 marks).
3. Give one reason an alternative does not fit (1 mark).

For regulator-driven, scope-fixed projects: pick linear. For uncertain scope with evolving requirements: pick iterative. For projects with both: pick hybrid.

golden_rules: Use 'linear' and 'iterative', never 'waterfall' or 'agile'. APM terminology only.
Memorise the four project phases: Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition. Two extended phases on top: Adoption, Benefits Realisation.
When asked 'which life cycle', justify with three reasons tied to the scenario, and explain why one alternative does not fit.
For a high-uncertainty IT project, pick iterative and pair it with the phrase 'allows objectives to evolve as learning and discovery take place'.

misconceptions.right: Iterative suits evolving scope; linear suits stable scope. The right choice depends on context, not fashion.
misconceptions.wrong: Iterative is the modern, better life cycle for every project.

misconceptions.right: Linear projects handle change through formal change control. They are less suited to constantly evolving scope, not change-resistant.
misconceptions.wrong: Linear projects can't handle any change.

misconceptions.right: An extended life cycle adds Adoption and Benefits Realisation phases beyond transition and close. Length is incidental.
misconceptions.wrong: An extended life cycle is just a longer project.

misconceptions.right: Hybrid combines linear and iterative deliberately. It requires more skill, not less, to manage multiple systems of working in parallel.
misconceptions.wrong: Hybrid means there are no rules.

misconceptions.right: Choice is shaped by organisational context, culture, project needs and stakeholder appetite. The sponsor and governance board are involved.
misconceptions.wrong: The life cycle choice is the project manager's decision alone.

worked_example.scenario: You are project manager on a regulatory change required by the Financial Conduct Authority. The regulator has given clear written expectations of the changes and wants regular updates on progress and on how you manage risk to customers. Penalties for missing the deadline are large.
worked_example.model_answer: (a) Linear life cycle. (b) Three reasons: (1) Greater control and governance, which the regulator's reporting demands require. (2) Requirements and outcomes are known upfront from the regulator's written expectations, so scope can be fixed. (3) Higher predictability and clearer scope-quality delivery, important when penalties for failure are significant. (c) One reason not to use iterative: iterative life cycles assume scope can evolve through learning, but the regulator's requirements are fixed and any deviation creates legal risk; iterative would also produce inconsistent reporting against the regulator's expected milestones.
